title: For the Birds
logline: Fifteen small blue birds share a telephone wire until one very big bird lands, and everything starts to bend.
why: There is no dialogue at all, so every joke is told with faces, feathers and a sagging wire. Colours, sizes and simple actions carry the whole story, which lets beginners follow without missing a word.
language: No spoken words, only bird sounds and music, so there is no accent or fast speech to worry about.
content: Cartoon slapstick: birds peck toes, the little birds fall and lose their feathers, but nobody is hurt and it is suitable for all ages.

scenes.title: Birds on the wire
scenes.task: Count the small birds on the wire. What colour are they?

scenes.title: The big bird arrives
scenes.task: The big bird waves at the others. Is he friendly or unfriendly? Show your answer with your face.

scenes.title: Toes and beaks
scenes.task: The little birds peck the big bird's toes. In one sentence, say why they are angry.

scenes.title: The slingshot
scenes.task: The wire jumps like a slingshot. Show with your hands what happens to the little birds.

words.ex: The birds sit on the wire.
A big bird lands on the wire.
The small birds are blue.
The small birds laugh at him.

words.def: a soft thing on a bird
words.ex: Feathers fall from the sky.
The big bird falls, but he is fine.

questions: How many small birds sit on the wire? Count them with your partner.
What colour are the small birds? Is the big bird the same colour?
Why do the small birds laugh at the big bird? Is that kind?
The small birds peck the big bird's toes. Is that a good idea? What happens next?
Would you like to sit on that wire with the birds? Why or why not?
In your country, do people laugh at someone who is different? What can we do about it?
The big bird laughs, but then he is kind. What does he do? Why do you think he helps?
Which moment made you laugh most? Show it to the group with your face.

quotes.note: A moment, not a line: his weight bends the wire.

quotes.note: A moment, not a line: the big bird is kind at the end.

quiz.q: Where do the birds sit?

quiz.why: Fifteen little blue birds share the wire.

quiz.q: What does the big bird do at the end?
options: He laughs and gives a leaf
quiz.why: He laughs at the birds with no feathers, then kindly offers a leaf.

roleplay.title: The wire

title: Lava
logline: A lonely volcano sings a song of hope to the sea every day, while a small volcano under the water listens and loves him.
why: The whole story is one slow, clear song, so there is no dialogue to follow and the bright pictures carry the feelings. The words repeat, and the volcanoes' faces show love, hope and sadness without translation.
language: The only words are sung slowly and clearly with a Hawaiian-style ukulele song; the singers hold long notes, so lines are easy to catch.
content: A lonely character feels sad and almost disappears, but the ending is happy; there is no violence and nothing frightening.

scenes.title: A lonely volcano
scenes.task: Look at Uku's face. How does he feel? Show the feeling with your face.

scenes.title: The song
scenes.task: Listen for the word lava. Put up one finger every time you hear it.

scenes.title: Under the sea

scenes.title: Two volcanoes
scenes.task: Describe the ending in three words. Is it happy, sad or funny? Say why.

In your country, is there a song about love or the sea? Can you hum it for the group?
Which part of the song did you like best? Say one word from it.

title: Hair Love
logline: A father tries to do his daughter's hair for the first time, with help from a video and one very lively head of curls.
why: The story is almost wordless: faces, hands, brushes and a phone video tell you everything, so beginners can follow without dialogue. The short lines are slow and simple, and the same hair words come back again and again.
language: A few short lines in warm American English, but most of the film is music and action, so the speed is never a problem.
content: A mother is in hospital with cancer and has lost her hair, shown gently, and the family hugs at the end; nothing is frightening.

scenes.title: At the hospital

title: The Present
logline: A boy gets a surprise present from his mother: a happy little puppy with three legs who wants only one thing, to play.
why: There is no dialogue, and the story is told through one room, one box and two faces, so the meaning is always visible. The puppy's actions repeat, run, fall, get up, bring the ball, which gives beginners useful present-simple language.
language: No spoken words at all; music and puppy sounds carry the story, so there is nothing fast to decode.
content: A puppy is rejected at first and the boy is unkind to it, and both the puppy and the boy have one leg; the ending is warm and nothing is frightening.

scenes.title: The box
scenes.task: What is in the box? Guess before the boy opens it.

title: Zootopia
logline: A small rabbit joins the police in a big city of animals and takes on a case that the bigger officers cannot solve.
why: The plot is a clear police case: find the missing animals, so learners always know what the characters want. Everyday city vocabulary, short jokes and a lot of visual humour keep A2 students inside the story even when a line is fast.
language: American English with many different animal voices; the sloth at the DMV speaks very slowly, the sheep speak softly, and a few characters use fast city slang.
content: Bullying in flashbacks, a child is scratched, and some animals turn scary and savage; there is cartoon threat and fear, but no blood.

scenes.title: The school play
scenes.task: Judy is a child in a school play. What does she say she wants to be? Listen for the word police.

scenes.title: The DMV
scenes.task: Count how many times Flash the sloth looks at the screen. Why is the scene funny?

scenes.title: Mr. Big
scenes.task: Who is Mr. Big? Why is Judy afraid of him? Predict: will he help her?

scenes.title: The museum
scenes.task: Watch Bellwether's face and listen to her voice. What do you learn about her?

Judy takes a hard case.

words.def: lost, not where it should be

words.def: an animal that other animals hunt

title: Moana
logline: A young girl from a Pacific island is chosen by the sea and sails out to find a demigod and bring back what he stole.
why: The story follows one clear journey with songs that repeat key words, so A2 learners can track the goal from island to island. The visuals explain the magic, and the dialogue is slow and warm, with jokes that work even when a word is new.
language: American English with Pacific island names and a few Polynesian words; the songs are clear but fast in places, and Maui speaks in a quick, joking voice.
content: A grandmother dies gently on screen, and a big lava monster chases the heroes; there is mild peril and grief, but no blood.

title: Inside Out
logline: Five feelings live inside a girl's head and try to help her after her family moves to a new city.
why: The film turns feelings into characters, so emotions are visible, named and repeated, which is perfect for A2 vocabulary work. The story is a clear journey back home, and the dialogue is short and funny, with visual jokes that carry the meaning.
language: American English, warm and clear; the five emotions speak in very different voices, with Joy fast and bright and Sadness slow and soft, which helps learners hear tone.
content: A child is very sad, runs away from home for a short time, and an imaginary friend fades away; there is grief and family tension, handled gently, and nothing violent.

scenes.title: The first memory
scenes.task: Watch Riley's first memory. What colour is it? Which feeling is with her?

scenes.title: The dinner
scenes.task: The family eats dinner. Which feelings take control? Act out one face.

scenes.task: Bing Bong does something kind. What is it? Say one sentence.

scenes.task: Riley talks to her parents. What does she say she feels?

Riley's family moves to a new city. What helps a person start again in a new place?
Which line from the film stayed with you? Say it in English, then say why.

quotes.quote: Take her to the moon for me, okay?

quiz.q: Who are the five emotions?
quiz.why: They all live and work in Riley's Headquarters.

quiz.q: Why is Riley sad at the start of the film?
options: Her family moves to a new city
quiz.why: The family leaves Minnesota for San Francisco, and everything feels wrong.

quiz.q: What is Bing Bong?
quiz.why: He is the friend Riley invented when she was small.

quiz.q: What happens to the personality islands?
quiz.why: Without Joy and Sadness, Riley's islands start to break and fall.

quiz.q: What does Riley do when she is very upset?
quiz.why: She takes a bus to Minnesota, then comes back and talks to her parents.

roleplay.title: Headquarters
roleplay.setting: A control room with five chairs and one big screen. Riley has just come home from school.

roles.brief: You want to fix everything and keep Riley happy. You speak fast and you smile a lot.
You want to sit down and feel it. You speak slowly and softly.
You are angry about the move and you want to shout. You speak in short, hot sentences.

roleplay.challenge: Let each feeling say one sentence about the same day. Then decide together what Riley will do.

quest.title: Station 1: Two cities
quest.task: Find the name of Riley's old city and her new city.

quest.title: Station 2: Word puzzle
quest.task: Which word means something you remember? Find it in the word list.

quest.title: Station 3: Your control desk
quest.task: Draw your own control desk with five feelings. Write the name of each one.

quest.title: Station 4: In order
quest.task: Put these in order: the family moves, Riley's first memory, Bing Bong fades, Riley cries to her parents.
quest.answer: first memory, family moves, Bing Bong fades, Riley cries

title: Kung Fu Panda
logline: A clumsy panda who loves kung fu is chosen to be the Dragon Warrior, and now he must learn to fight without losing himself.
why: The story is a simple training plot with clear goals: be chosen, train, face the enemy. Food, family and daily routines give A2 learners concrete vocabulary, and the jokes are visual enough to follow even when the words are new.
language: American English with a few Chinese words and names; Master Shifu speaks slowly and formally, Po talks fast and makes jokes, and the Furious Five speak in short, clear lines.
content: Cartoon fighting, kicks and falls, and a scary snow leopard villain; nobody bleeds, but younger children may find the prison and fight scenes loud.

scenes.title: The noodle shop
scenes.task: Po works in his father's shop. What is his job? Where does he work?

scenes.title: The Dragon Warrior
scenes.task: Oogway chooses the Dragon Warrior. Who does everyone expect? Who is chosen?

scenes.title: Training with food
scenes.task: Shifu trains Po with dumplings. Why does this work? Watch Po's face.

scenes.title: The blank scroll
scenes.task: The Dragon Scroll is empty. What does Po see in it? What does that mean?

words.def: a big black and white bear
words.ex: Po is a big panda.
Po carries a bowl of noodles.
Po has a dream of kung fu.
Po trains every day.
The Dragon Warrior is a hero.
You must believe in yourself.

questions: What is Po's job at the start? What does he dream about?
Why do the Furious Five not want Po at the Jade Palace? Are they fair to him?
Oogway says there are no accidents. What does he mean? Do you agree?
Shifu trains Po with food. Is that a good way to teach? Why does it work?
Would you like to train at the Jade Palace? What would be the hardest part for you?
In your country, is there a traditional sport or fighting style? How is it taught?
Po's father wants him to sell noodles. Is it wrong to want a different life from your parents?
Which line made you laugh? Say it in English with the same feeling.

gaps.line: There is no secret ___.
I'm not a big fat panda. I'm ___ big fat panda.
Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery, but today is a ___.
There are no ___.
To make something special, you just have to ___ it's special.

quotes.quote: There are no accidents.
quotes.note: Oogway says it to Shifu when Po falls into the palace.

quotes.quote: I'm not a big fat panda. I'm THE big fat panda.
quotes.note: Po's answer when Tai Lung calls him a big fat panda.

quotes.quote: Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery, but today is a gift.
quotes.note: Oogway's advice under the peach tree.

quiz.q: What animal is Po?
quiz.why: Po is a panda who works in a noodle shop.

quiz.q: Who chooses the Dragon Warrior?
quiz.why: Oogway points to Po at the tournament.

quiz.q: What is the name of the villain?
quiz.why: Tai Lung is the snow leopard who wants the Dragon Scroll.

quiz.q: What is inside the Dragon Scroll?
quiz.why: The scroll is blank and shows Po his own reflection.

quiz.q: Who is Po's father?
quiz.why: Mr. Ping is the goose who adopted Po and runs the noodle shop.

roleplay.title: The noodle shop
roleplay.setting: A small noodle shop in the Valley of Peace. Po is serving, Mr. Ping is cooking, a customer is waiting.

roles.brief: You dream of kung fu and you are not good at serving. You drop things and say sorry.
You love your son and your noodles. You want him to stay and take over the shop.
You are hungry and in a hurry. You only want a bowl of noodles.

roleplay.challenge: Play it twice: once as a comedy, once as a sad scene about a son who wants a different life.

quest.title: Station 1: The five
quest.task: Find the names of the five fighters in the Furious Five.

quest.title: Station 2: Word puzzle
quest.task: Which word means a very brave fighter? Find it in the word list.

quest.title: Station 3: New move
quest.task: Invent one new kung fu move. Give it a name and show it in slow motion.

quest.title: Station 4: In order
quest.task: Put these in order: Po is chosen, Po works in the noodle shop, Po opens the Dragon Scroll, Po fights Tai Lung.
quest.answer: noodle shop, chosen, scroll, fights Tai Lung
